part_title: DynamoDB Integrations, DAX, TTL and Vector Index Freshness

scenes.title: PartiQL for DynamoDB
scenes.narration: PartiQL gives DynamoDB a SQL-compatible statement language for operations on items, and this slide shows what that means in practice. The four boxes on the left contain SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements. In the centre, the same PartiQL statement can be sent from the AWS console, an SDK, or an API call, using the supported execution interfaces. Follow the arrow to the Orders DynamoDB table on the right, where items still use DynamoDB's ordinary primary keys. This is an important nuance: PartiQL changes how we express requests; it does not turn DynamoDB into a general relational database or eliminate partition-key access patterns. The bottom orange callout reminds us that performance and cost still depend on the table's key design, indexes, and how many items are accessed. Use PartiQL when SQL-like syntax suits the integration, but verify that queries target efficient access patterns and avoid expensive broad scans.

scenes.title: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
scenes.narration: Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator, usually called DAX, is the managed in-memory cache shown in the centre of this diagram. Follow the numbered arrows. The application asks for an item, and the request reaches the DAX cluster. On a cache hit, DAX returns the result directly, typically with much lower latency than a trip to the database. On a cache miss, DAX reads the item from DynamoDB, returns the result, and can cache it for a later read. The cluster is shown spanning multiple Availability Zones for high availability, while the lower-right card illustrates a default item-cache time to live of five minutes. The precise caching behaviour depends on the API operation and configuration. DAX is intended for suitable DynamoDB read patterns and works with supported DynamoDB-compatible client access. It is not an automatic fix for poor partition keys or a replacement for DynamoDB storage. Its strongest use cases are repeated, latency-sensitive reads that benefit from caching.

scenes.title: DAX Versus ElastiCache
scenes.narration: The next slide contrasts two AWS caching choices that may look similar at first. On the orange side, DAX is purpose-built for DynamoDB items and compatible read/query results. The application uses a DAX-compatible client, and DAX manages the cache interactions with DynamoDB. On the cyan side, ElastiCache provides a more general-purpose in-memory cache for application objects, sessions, computed results, or other data, using a supported cache engine such as Redis or Memcached. The lower use-case panel explains the decision. Choose DAX when your primary goal is accelerating supported DynamoDB read access without writing a separate application caching layer. Choose ElastiCache when the application needs arbitrary cached values or custom caching rules beyond DynamoDB items. In either case, consider how cached data becomes stale and what consistency the business requires. Faster reads do not automatically mean the latest write is visible through every cache path.

scenes.title: DynamoDB Time to Live
scenes.narration: Time to Live, or TTL, allows DynamoDB to remove expired items automatically. Look at the four numbered steps at the top. First, write a numeric Unix epoch timestamp in a designated TTL attribute, such as ttl. Second, once the current time passes that timestamp, the item becomes eligible for expiration. Third, DynamoDB performs deletion asynchronously, which means expired data can remain visible for some time. Fourth, if DynamoDB Streams is enabled, TTL-driven removals can appear as change events. The bottom illustration follows one item from a timestamped record, through expiration, to an eventual delete event. The key takeaway is that TTL is not an exact scheduling mechanism and does not guarantee an item disappears at the precise second shown. If an application must never return expired sessions or temporary data, it should also check the timestamp during reads. This pattern is useful for session cleanup, temporary tokens, and data with predictable retention windows.

scenes.title: DynamoDB in GenAI
scenes.narration: Here is a realistic way to combine DynamoDB with a generative AI model. Start with the user question on the left: What's the status of my order? The application looks up the user's session or current structured facts in DynamoDB, using an appropriate user or session identifier. Look at the centre storage box, which includes chat history, session metadata, and user or order facts. The application sends only the needed context to a model in Amazon Bedrock, shown on the right, so the generated answer can include current application information. Notice the purple caution below. DynamoDB is not serving as a native nearest-neighbour vector search engine in this architecture. If the application also needs semantic retrieval over documents, the bottom path uses a separate vector index such as OpenSearch, Aurora with an appropriate extension, or another suitable store. The architecture combines structured state with retrieved knowledge, rather than expecting one data service to do every job.

scenes.title: DynamoDB to OpenSearch
scenes.narration: This slide shows an event-driven integration between two different kinds of storage. On the left, DynamoDB holds operational records, such as order details and catalog information. When those records change, a replication or integration pipeline captures the changes and transforms them for indexing. Follow the arrows to Amazon OpenSearch, where records can be made searchable by full text, selected metadata, and vector embeddings when configured. An application then retrieves relevant indexed context and passes that context to Amazon Bedrock for a grounded response. The three numbered boxes at the bottom clarify responsibility. DynamoDB remains the operational source for keyed reads and writes. The integration updates the search representation. OpenSearch serves retrieval queries, not necessarily the original transactional write. Synchronization can be near real time or eventually consistent depending on the pipeline. Handle deletes, retries, ordering, and permissions explicitly; otherwise a search answer may reflect stale or already removed data.

scenes.title: Keep Vector Stores Fresh
scenes.narration: A retrieval application is only as current as its index. Follow the four stages across the top. First, source records are created, modified, or deleted. A change-detection step identifies what happened, often through event notifications or timestamps. Third, a change handler creates or updates an embedding for new content, or prepares a deletion for content that no longer exists. Finally, the vector store applies the corresponding update. The two panels underneath show complementary strategies. An event-driven pipeline reacts quickly to changes in databases, objects, or application records. A scheduled reconciliation job scans the source again to find missed events and correct index drift. The small banner at the bottom gives a crucial design detail: preserve a stable source record ID with each vector. Without that link, it's difficult to upsert changed records or reliably delete stale vectors. The best production design usually combines prompt updates with periodic correctness checks.

scenes.title: Event-Driven Sync Pattern
scenes.narration: Now we have the event-driven freshness pattern expanded into an AWS workflow. On the upper row, an object is added or changed in S3. EventBridge matches the relevant S3 event and routes it to AWS Lambda. The Lambda connector reads the source, extracts content, splits it into chunks, generates embeddings using a model, and upserts the resulting records into the vector index. Follow the dashed loop below. Retries and idempotency are needed because an event may be delivered more than once or a processing step may fail partway through. The separate lower red path handles S3 object deletion: the integration finds the vectors associated with that object and removes them. Notice why source identifiers and index metadata matter. A delete event must remove the right vectors, not every item with similar text. With retries, permissions, and suitable event filtering, this pattern can keep a RAG index aligned with an evolving document repository.

scenes.title: Vector Index Rebuild
scenes.narration: Not every change can be handled safely with a small incremental update. This slide demonstrates a full index rebuild with minimal disruption. At step one, a scheduled EventBridge rule triggers a rebuild. Step two uses AWS Batch or another processing worker to read current source content and create a refreshed dataset. Step three generates embeddings and loads a completely new vector index. Step four validates that new index by checking document counts and retrieval quality against representative queries. Step five switches the application's read alias or configured endpoint from the old index to the new one. Only after the replacement is healthy does step six retire the old index. The dotted bottom line shows users continuing to query the old index throughout most of the process. That prevents rebuilding from becoming an immediate outage. Use a stable routing layer and rollback plan so a failed validation does not force users onto a broken index.

scenes.title: Reranking in Bedrock
scenes.narration: Our final video slide shows how reranking can improve a retrieval workflow after the first search. At the left, the user asks how to set up VPC endpoints. The initial retrieval stage returns several candidate chunks from a knowledge source, but their original ordering may not match what the user needs. The centre reranker compares those candidate passages with the query and assigns relevance scores. Look at the blue results on the right. The candidates are reordered, with the highest-scoring chunks selected as the context for the generative model. The model then generates its answer using that more focused evidence. The lower cards show two approaches: calling an eligible reranking model through the Bedrock Rerank API, or using reranking through supported Knowledge Bases retrieval workflows. Reranking adds model calls, latency, and cost, so it should be evaluated against answer quality and retrieval metrics. It can improve selection from a good candidate pool, but cannot recover evidence that was never retrieved in the first place.
